sources.name: NASA software classification

sources.inspected: yes: page fetched 2026-10-03 through a fetch tool that returns a model-made extraction; quotations are as that tool returned them and were not compared character by character with the page. Appendix D and Chapter 2 only. The extraction reported classes A to F and the sentence that requirements and rigor are 'scaled back for lower software classes' and that an ambiguous case takes 'the higher of the classes'. The mapping matrix itself (Appendix C) was not opened.
sources.mechanism: Classify once by consequence of failure; the class selects which requirements apply; an ambiguous case takes the higher class; relief from a requirement is recorded against the same matrix and signed by a named authority.
sources.minimum_version: A small number of classes defined by consequence, a tie rule (higher wins), and a table of what each class adds.
sources.bureaucratic_if: Six classes, a matrix of more than a hundred requirement rows, and signature chains for every relief.
sources.kads_constraint: Three levels, the lowest of which requires nothing; KADS defines the levels by consequence and leaves criteria and classifier to the adoption note; the level selects record content, not process.

sources.name: NASA life-cycle reviews and readiness reviews
sources.citation: NPR 7123.1D, Appendix G (entrance and success criteria; ORR, MRR/FRR, CDR, PDR; G.1.2 tailoring)
sources.inspected: yes: page fetched 2026-10-03 through a fetch tool that returns a model-made extraction; quotations are as that tool returned them and were not compared character by character with the page. Appendix G only; the criteria tables were summarized by the tool, and the quoted success criteria were not checked against the tables.
sources.mechanism: A readiness review has entrance criteria (what must exist before the question is asked) and success criteria (what a GO asserts), so GO is a conclusion against stated criteria. Tailoring of criteria is expected.
sources.minimum_version: State the claim that 'ready' asserts and the evidence for it, separately from the decision to proceed.
sources.bureaucratic_if: A review board, a fixed review sequence, and a criteria table per review.
sources.kads_constraint: KADS records the claim, its evidence, and the choice as distinct statements in one decision record (clause 7.3 a, b). It does not require that a review be held.

sources.name: NASA Technical Authority, Formal Dissent, waivers and deviations
sources.citation: NPR 7120.5F, Chapter 3, sections 3.3 (Technical Authority), 3.4 (Formal Dissent), 3.5 (tailoring, waivers, deviations, Non-Applicable)
sources.inspected: yes: page fetched 2026-10-03 through a fetch tool that returns a model-made extraction; quotations are as that tool returned them and were not compared character by character with the page. Chapter 3 only. Section numbers are as the tool reported them.
sources.mechanism: (1) Three positions on a decision: agree, disagree but support, or disagree and raise a Formal Dissent, which is documented and carried upward. (2) Relief from a requirement is dispositioned by the level that set the requirement. (3) A requirement that cannot apply is recorded as Non-Applicable instead of being silently skipped. (4) Authority independent of the programme.
sources.minimum_version: A dissent that could change the choice is written down with the reason it did not prevail; an exception names the requirement and who accepted the risk.
sources.bureaucratic_if: An independent authority chain, appeal levels up to the head of the organization, and separate waiver and deviation forms.
sources.kads_constraint: KADS keeps only the record: disagreement recorded before acceptance stays in the record (7.3 h); an exception names requirement, risk, and acceptor (7.4 a). No veto, no appeal chain, no distinction between waiver and deviation.

candidates.title: Rigor proportional to consequence
candidates.problem: One fixed level of documentation is either too heavy for small changes or too light for dangerous ones, so teams either abandon it or apply it as ritual.
candidates.failure_mode: A password-policy change and a typo fix receive the same record; or every change must queue for the same review, as the SRE book reports for the simple PRR model (lead times of quarters).
candidates.observed_case: Public: Google SRE chapter 32 (PRR did not scale) and chapter 27 (low-risk launches moved to 'an almost trivial checklist'). KADS history: four challengers judged the first 0.6.0 draft too large. In KADS adoption: anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: Authors spend recording effort where being wrong is costly and nothing where it is not.
candidates.rationale: NPR 7150.2D scales requirements by class; the SRE launch checklist does the same informally. The principle is also the brief's guiding idea and matches the KADS design constraint in foundations.md.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: State the principle once in the design rationale; make it operative only through 7.2 and the table in 7.3. No separate rule.
candidates.wording: No normative text. One sentence for docs/foundations.md under Design constraint: 'Where KADS asks for more from a record, it asks in proportion to the consequence of the record being wrong; the assurance profile (section 7) is the only place where that scale is explicit.'
candidates.could_amend: docs/foundations.md, Design constraint paragraph.
candidates.tradeoffs: A principle with no clause is easy to ignore; a clause would duplicate 7.2.
candidates.weakest_point: Proportionality is already implicit in 'material claim' (section 2); a challenger can say the sentence adds nothing.

admission.failure: Uniform ceremony leads to abandonment or ritual. Observed publicly (SRE PRR scaling); anticipated only in KADS adoption.
admission.property: None directly; it is a design constraint on the standard, not on a corpus.
admission.detection: Not detectable as a rule; that is why it is guidance.
admission.cost: Nothing on upgrade. Nothing for a ten-line how-to.

candidates.title: No significant decision without rationale
candidates.problem: A reader finds what was decided and who decided it but not why, so cannot tell whether the decision still applies when conditions change.
candidates.failure_mode: A decision is reopened or silently reversed because nobody can tell which constraint it answered; or it is kept after its reason has gone.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: docs/decision-guide.md already instructs authors reconstructing old decisions to 'mark unknown authority or rationale', which records that the gap occurs. Clause 4.6 requires authority and effective date and is silent on reasons. No adopter report: anticipated in adoption.
candidates.behavior: Reasons are written at the time of the choice, or their absence is stated.
candidates.rationale: Nygard's ADR puts context and consequences beside the decision in one or two pages. Clause 4.6 already makes two decision fields mandatory; rationale is the third and the one the epistemic test in the brief depends on.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: One sentence in clause 4.6, with the escape 'or state that they are not recorded' so that historical decisions can conform without invention (clause 3.3.3).
candidates.wording: Add to clause 4.6 after the authority sentence: 'An accepted decision MUST state the reasons for the choice, or state that they are not recorded.'
candidates.could_amend: Clause 4.6 (tracked-record profile). No new clause.
candidates.tradeoffs: Breaking for tracked-record corpora whose accepted decisions carry no reasons; the migration is one line per such record. Does not reach decisions that are not tracked records.
candidates.weakest_point: The requirement checks presence, not quality: 'because we agreed' conforms. And 'significant' is not defined outside section 7, so the sentence binds every accepted tracked decision, including small ones.

admission.failure: A later reader cannot assess whether a decision still holds. Observed as a known gap in the decision guide; no adopter case.
admission.property: History is preserved; a material claim has an identifiable basis.
admission.detection: Reading one page: an accepted decision with no reasons and no statement of their absence.
admission.cost: On upgrade: add reasons or 'reasons not recorded' to each accepted tracked decision. A ten-line how-to: nothing.

candidates.title: No GO without evidence
candidates.problem: A statement that a change is ready is written as a decision ('approved to ship') with no claim that could be checked, so approval substitutes for evidence.
candidates.failure_mode: The reader cannot separate 'we believed it works, on this evidence' from 'someone allowed it', and after a failure cannot tell which was wrong.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Volume 1, Chapter V, finding 4 (a recommendation reversed 'contrary to the views of its engineers'): the GO existed, the supporting claim did not. In KADS adoption: anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: GO is written as a conclusion with evidence, followed by a separately attributed choice.
candidates.rationale: NPR 7123.1D Appendix G gives every readiness review success criteria, so that GO asserts something. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2 (not inspected) separates claim, argument, and evidence. KADS already separates finding, recommendation, and decision in the decision guide, and clause 5.6 forbids representing execution as satisfaction of a criterion.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (a) and (b): the claim is stated separately from the choice, with its evidence and what the evidence does not cover.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [items (a) and (b)]
candidates.could_amend: Clause 3.3.1 already requires a basis for material factual claims; 7.3 (a) makes the readiness claim explicit so that 3.3.1 has something to bind.
candidates.tradeoffs: Adds two statements to every significant decision record. Does not stop a team from shipping without evidence; it makes the absence visible.
candidates.weakest_point: KADS cannot enforce the principle as worded. A record that says 'claim: ready; evidence: none' conforms. The benefit is only that this is now legible.

admission.failure: Approval is read as evidence. Observed publicly (Challenger); anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: A material claim has an identifiable basis; nothing is stated more firmly than its support.
admission.detection: Reading one page: a record at significant level whose claim and evidence are absent or merged with the approval.
admission.cost: Nothing on upgrade unless the profile is adopted. A ten-line how-to: nothing.

candidates.title: No exception without explicit risk acceptance
candidates.problem: Departures from a rule accumulate as habits. Nobody chose them, nobody owns the risk, and they do not end.
candidates.failure_mode: A temporary workaround becomes permanent; a requirement is believed to hold when it has been waived for months.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Chapter V, finding 2, on waived launch constraints, and Chapter VI on a constraint waived for each subsequent flight. KADS history: conformance.md already requires an exception record for departures from KADS clauses; no case of a missing one is recorded.
candidates.behavior: A departure is written down once, with the person or role who accepted the risk and an end date.
candidates.rationale: NPR 7120.5F section 3.5 dispositions relief at the level that set the requirement. KADS conformance already demands clause, scope, reason, consequence, responsible role, and review condition. 7.4 extends that existing object from KADS clauses to any requirement a project treats as binding.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.4 (a): six fields, the same six that conformance already lists.
candidates.wording: 7.4 (a) An exception MUST identify the requirement departed from, its scope, the reason, the risk accepted, who accepted it, and an expiry date or review condition. (b) An exception stated to be permanent SHOULD say why the requirement is not changed instead. (c) An exception whose expiry date has passed without a recorded renewal MUST NOT be presented as in force. (d) Exceptions in force SHOULD be listed where the requirement is stated or be reachable from the corpus entry point. An exception to a KADS clause is the exception that conformance already requires; this clause adds no field to it. [item (a)]
candidates.could_amend: docs/conformance.md, Review outcome, second paragraph: the same fields, limited there to KADS clauses.
candidates.tradeoffs: Writing exceptions down can legitimize them. A team with many informal departures faces a backlog when it adopts the profile.
candidates.weakest_point: KADS has no observed case of an unrecorded exception in an adopting project, and whether 'a requirement the project treats as binding' is identifiable enough for a reviewer is untested.

admission.failure: A reader relies on a requirement that is not in force for some scope. Observed publicly; anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: A statement's scope is known; current guidance can be found.
admission.detection: Reading one exception record for the six fields. An unrecorded exception is not detectable by reading; that part stays outside the rule.
admission.cost: Nothing on upgrade unless the profile is adopted; then each known exception gets the six fields.

candidates.title: Absence of failure is not evidence of correctness
candidates.problem: 'No incidents so far' is offered as evidence that a change, design, or exception is safe, without saying whether a failure would have been noticed.
candidates.failure_mode: Each uneventful repetition raises confidence in a condition that was never tested; the anomaly becomes the baseline.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Chapter VI (O-ring erosion accepted as experience accumulated; the comparison on the eve of launch covered only flights with damage). CAIB on foam loss: unverified, not inspected. KADS history: clause 5.7 was adopted from adopter lesson 3, where a negative result was stated more broadly than the inspection supported; this is the same error applied to failure.
candidates.behavior: A no-failure statement carries its scope: what was watched, for how long, and how a failure would have appeared.
candidates.rationale: Chaos engineering (principlesofchaos.org) builds confidence by trying to disprove a steady-state hypothesis. Clause 5.7 already scopes negative results in research reports; a no-failure claim is a negative result outside a research report.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (i), one conditional sentence. It binds only when the evidence offered is absence of failure.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [item (i)]
candidates.could_amend: Clause 5.7 could carry it if the decision record were treated as a research report; it is cleaner to cite 5.7 from the guide and state the rule where decision evidence is listed.
candidates.tradeoffs: Honest teams with good monitoring write one more sentence. The rule cannot make anyone look for failures.
candidates.weakest_point: Arguably already covered by 3.3.1 plus 5.7; a challenger can call it a restatement. It is kept because the Challenger case is exactly this error made by competent people.

admission.failure: A reader takes a quiet period as proof. Observed publicly and, in the form of over-broad negative results, in KADS adoption (lesson 3).
admission.property: Nothing is stated more firmly than its support.
admission.detection: Reading one page: a no-failure statement with no observation scope or detection means.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: Critical changes consider off-nominal behavior
candidates.problem: Records of critical changes describe the intended path only, so the reader cannot tell whether failure was thought about or how it would have been noticed.
candidates.failure_mode: A failure occurs that nobody had named, with no detection in place, and the record gives a later investigator nothing to compare against.
candidates.observed_case: Public: GitLab postmortem of 2017-01-31 (backup failures went unnoticed because the failure notifications were themselves rejected). In KADS adoption: anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: The author of a critical change writes down how it could fail and how that would be seen.
candidates.rationale: FMEA (IEC 60812, not inspected) asks failure mode, effect, detection. The SRE PRR checklist asks whether failures are instrumented. The brief's six questions reduce to two that a record can answer: how can it fail, how would we know. Propagation and containment are answered in 7.3 (e).
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (f), critical level only, prose, no worksheet.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [item (f)]
candidates.could_amend: Clause 3.5.4 (a) covers irreversible effects of procedure steps; it does not reach a decision record.
candidates.tradeoffs: At critical level only, so a significant change may still ship with no failure analysis recorded. A weak answer ('could fail in unknown ways; monitoring') conforms.
candidates.weakest_point: This is the candidate closest to prescribing engineering thought instead of record content. The defence is that it asks for a statement, not an analysis method.

admission.failure: An investigator cannot tell what the deciders foresaw. Anticipated in adoption; observed publicly.
admission.property: A material claim has an identifiable basis (the claim being that the change is ready).
admission.detection: Reading one page: a critical record with no failure and detection statement.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: Recovery designed before deployment
candidates.problem: A change is recorded as ready with no statement of how it would be undone, or with a recovery path that was never exercised.
candidates.failure_mode: Rollback is found not to exist, or not to work, at the moment it is needed; an irreversible step is discovered during the change.
candidates.observed_case: Public: GitLab 2017-01-31, where no usable backup existed and the postmortem asks 'Why was the backup procedure not tested on a regular basis?'. KADS: clause 3.5.4 (c) already addresses unexecuted procedures; no adopter case.
candidates.behavior: The record states the recovery path, or says plainly that there is none, before the change is accepted.
candidates.rationale: SRE canarying and staged rollout limit exposure; clause 3.5.4 already requires irreversible effects to be stated in procedures. Irreversibility is one of the two decisive classification factors in 7.2, which is how 'irreversibility raises assurance' is implemented.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (e) at significant and critical level. Whether the path was exercised is not a new rule: a statement that recovery was tested falls under clause 3.3.5, and an untested runbook under 3.5.4 (c). The guide says so.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [item (e)]; guidance sentence for the decision guide: 'A recovery path named in a decision record is a procedure; say whether it has been executed (clauses 3.3.5 and 3.5.4 c).'
candidates.could_amend: Clause 3.5.4 (b) and (c) carry the procedure side already.
candidates.tradeoffs: The record can state a recovery path that is fiction. KADS names no technique (flags, canaries, backups), so the brief's list lives only in guidance.
candidates.weakest_point: 'Designed before deployment' is a timing requirement on engineering; the record rule only requires the statement in the decision record. A record written afterwards conforms if it is honest about dates.

admission.failure: A reader assumes a change can be reversed. Observed publicly.
admission.property: A statement's scope is known; nothing is stated more firmly than its support.
admission.detection: Reading one page: no recovery statement, or 'tested' without the 3.3.5 particulars.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: High-risk decisions receive independent challenge
candidates.problem: A reader cannot tell whether anyone other than the authors examined the reasoning behind a critical decision, and takes an approval for an examination.
candidates.failure_mode: A self-reviewed, or agent-reviewed, critical decision reads as independently checked.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: the 0.6.0 gate found review claims written without knowledge of what was reviewed (changelog 0.6.0, Corrected), and record J-029 notes that review by a second agent can be presented as independent review. No adopter case.
candidates.behavior: Authors of critical decisions seek a challenge because its absence must be written down.
candidates.rationale: NASA Technical Authority (NPR 7120.5F section 3.3) provides independent oversight; IV&V scales independence with class (prior knowledge). J-029 rejected an independence requirement as governance outside KADS and set its reopening condition as 'that would be a profile'. This is that profile, and it still asks for disclosure only.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (g): who other than the authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did. Clause 3.3.4 already forces automated review to be named as such.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [item (g)]
candidates.could_amend: Clause 3.3.5 covers statements that a review occurred; it does not require saying that none occurred. 7.3 (g) adds only the negative statement, at critical level.
candidates.tradeoffs: The principle says 'require'; the mechanism only discloses. A team can write 'no one did' and conform.
candidates.weakest_point: A challenger will say this fails the candidate as written. The defence: clause 3.6.3 says KADS does not grant authority to approve decisions, and record J-029 rejected an independence requirement on that ground in the 0.6.0 evaluation of 2026-10-03.

admission.failure: A reader over-trusts an unexamined critical decision. Observed in KADS's own history as invented review statements.
admission.property: Nothing is stated more firmly than its support.
admission.detection: Reading one page: a critical record silent on examination.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: Technical dissent stays traceable
candidates.problem: Disagreement raised before a decision disappears from the accepted record, so the decision reads as unanimous.
candidates.failure_mode: A later reader cannot find the objection that turned out to be right, or learns of it only from memory.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Chapter V: the deciders 'were unaware ... of the continuing opposition of the engineers' (as quoted in a search result of that chapter) and finding 4. KADS history: decisions/standards/README.md keeps 'Recorded dissents that did not prevail' for the 0.6.0 evaluation; that is the practice, not a failure.
candidates.behavior: Objections are written into the record with the reason they did not prevail; nobody has to win to be recorded.
candidates.rationale: RFC 7282: issues are addressed, not necessarily accommodated, and numbers do not settle it. NPR 7120.5F section 3.4 gives three positions including disagree-but-support. KADS clause 3.3.2 already requires known contradictions to be disclosed, and both decision outlines mention dissent.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3 (h) plus the non-requirement sentence 'The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement.' No veto, no escalation path, no dissent record type.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1). [item (h) and the sentence on absence of recorded disagreement]
candidates.could_amend: Clause 3.3.2 ('Known contradictions ... MUST be disclosed') arguably covers it; 7.3 (h) makes the application to decisions explicit at critical level. For lower levels the decision guide sentence stays advisory.
candidates.tradeoffs: Binds only disagreement that was recorded somewhere before acceptance; oral dissent never written down is outside it. At significant level it stays advisory.
candidates.weakest_point: Detection requires comparing the accepted record with earlier drafts or discussion, which is 'comparing two', not 'reading one page'.

admission.failure: A decision reads as uncontested. Observed publicly.
admission.property: History is preserved; known contradictions are disclosed.
admission.detection: Comparing the accepted record with its draft history or the linked discussion.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: Incidents change the system, not only the documentation
candidates.problem: An incident write-up lists lessons and is filed; nothing shows whether any lesson changed a requirement, test, monitor, or runbook.
candidates.failure_mode: The same incident recurs; the postmortem exists and is 'complete'.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Chapter VI (the O-ring problem was closed in tracking on request while unresolved). SRE book chapter 15: 'An unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed.' KADS adoption feedback of 2026-10-02 is the positive form: six lessons, each with a disposition and a location. No adopter failure case.
candidates.behavior: Each lesson ends in a visible disposition, including 'no change, because'.
candidates.rationale: The SRE postmortem goal includes that preventive actions are put in place. KADS's own adoption-feedback note already uses a lesson, disposition, where table.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.5 (a): one disposition per lesson, four allowed values, each with its link or reason. The incident record is an investigation record; no new type.
candidates.wording: 7.5 (a) A record of an incident investigation MUST state, for each lesson it draws, one disposition: a change made, with a link to it; a change pending, with a link to where it is tracked; a risk accepted, naming who accepted it; or no change, with the reason. (b) Where an incident shows that an assumption or evidence relied on by a recorded decision did not hold, the incident record SHOULD link to that decision. (c) A record at the critical level SHOULD state when and how its outcome will be checked, and later what was observed. [item (a)]
candidates.could_amend: No existing clause addresses lessons. Clause 3.4.3 names an incident as a review trigger, which is the hook.
candidates.tradeoffs: KADS cannot make the change happen. 'Pending, tracked at X' can stay pending forever; the rule only keeps that visible.
candidates.weakest_point: The candidate's strong form ('not closed until') is a process rule on closure that KADS cannot own. The proposal deliberately weakens it to disclosure.

admission.failure: A reader assumes a known lesson was applied. Observed publicly; the positive practice is observed in KADS.
admission.property: Current guidance can be found; history is preserved.
admission.detection: Reading one page: a lesson with no disposition.
admission.cost: Nothing unless the profile is adopted.

candidates.title: Three assurance levels
candidates.problem: Without a shared scale, 'proportional' is decided afresh by every author and cannot be reviewed.
candidates.failure_mode: A dangerous change is treated as ordinary because nothing forced the question; or everything is treated as dangerous.
candidates.observed_case: Public: NPR 7150.2D classes; SRE low-risk launch category (30 percent of reviews by 2008, as the tool extracted). In KADS adoption: anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: The author asks two questions before writing: can it be undone, and how far does it reach.
candidates.rationale: Three levels is the smallest scale with a level that requires nothing, a level that requires the basics, and a level for the irreversible. NASA uses six; ITIL three change types (not inspected).
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.2 with three one-line definitions. Two decisive factors in the definitions (reversibility; reach beyond what the team can itself restore). The other eight factors of the brief are examples in the guide of what raises a level. The project states criteria and classifier in its adoption note; the default classifier is the author of record of the decision, and the accepting authority can raise the level.
candidates.wording: 7.2 (a) A project applying this profile MUST state in its adoption note the criteria by which it assigns the levels routine, significant, and critical, and who assigns them. (b) A record made under clause 7.3 MUST state its level and the factor that decided it. (c) Where criteria point to different levels, the higher SHOULD be assigned. A project MAY map existing local classes, such as change types or severity classes, to these levels.
candidates.could_amend: None; this is the one genuinely new concept. The adoption note (clause 6.1) carries the criteria.
candidates.tradeoffs: Classification is itself a decision before every decision. Levels invite gaming downward. The profile cannot detect a critical change left unrecorded as routine.
candidates.weakest_point: A reviewer cannot detect under-classification of something never recorded. The level is a new defined term and must pass admission question 7 with only public cases.

admission.failure: Recording effort is misallocated. Anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: A statement's scope is known (the level tells the reader how much to expect from the record).
admission.detection: Reading the adoption note for criteria; reading one record for its level and deciding factor.
admission.cost: Nothing unless adopted. On adoption: one paragraph in the adoption note.

candidates.title: Decision assurance structure
candidates.problem: The parts of a justified decision (claim, evidence, assumptions, risk, authority, dissent, outcome) are scattered or missing, so reconstruction fails.
candidates.failure_mode: Six months later the choice is known but not what was believed or which risk was knowingly taken.
candidates.observed_case: Same public cases as P-03 and P-09. KADS: the decision outline already has authority, rationale, alternatives, validation, and revisit sections; assumptions and accepted risk are mentioned but not required.
candidates.behavior: Authors fill a short fixed set of statements whose number grows with level.
candidates.rationale: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2 (not inspected): claim, argument, evidence, assumptions. Nygard: short record. Clause 4.6 already carries decision, authority, and effective date; clause 5.2 is the precedent for a 'MUST make the following discoverable' list.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.3: five items at significant, three more at critical, one conditional. Of the brief's nine fields: decision and authority are clause 4.6; rationale is the 4.6 amendment; outcome is 7.5 (c); the rest are 7.3.
candidates.wording: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the claim the decision rests on, such as that the change is ready, stated separately from the choice to proceed; (b) the evidence for that claim and what the evidence does not cover; (c) the assumptions relied on; (d) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them; (e) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be. At the critical level the record MUST also make discoverable: (f) how the change could fail and how the failure would be detected; (g) who other than its authors examined the reasoning and what they found, or that no one did; (h) each disagreement recorded before acceptance that could change the choice, with the reason it did not prevail. (i) Where the evidence in (b) is that no failure has been observed, the record MUST state what was observed, over what period or exposure, and how a failure would have been detected. The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement. Evidence is linked, not copied (clause 3.2.1).
candidates.could_amend: Clause 4.6 carries three of the nine fields already; putting all of them there would impose them on every tracked decision, which violates proportionality.
candidates.tradeoffs: Eight lettered items is the largest clause in the specification after 5.2. 'Evidence referenced, not copied' is clause 3.2.1 restated.
candidates.weakest_point: The list checks presence, not adequacy; a challenger can call it a template promoted to a rule.

admission.failure: Decisions cannot be reconstructed. Observed publicly; anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: A material claim has an identifiable basis; history is preserved.
admission.detection: Reading one page against the lettered list.
admission.cost: Nothing unless adopted.

candidates.title: Readiness record
candidates.problem: Readiness is asserted in chat or a ticket and leaves no reconstructable statement.
candidates.failure_mode: After a failed launch nobody can say what 'ready' meant.
candidates.observed_case: Public: NPR 7123.1D Appendix G gives readiness reviews explicit success criteria; SRE chapter 27 on launch checklists. In KADS adoption: anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: The team answers the readiness questions in the record of the decision to proceed.
candidates.rationale: The eight questions of the brief map one to one onto existing fields: what is changing (decision statement, 4.6); why we believe it works (7.3 a); evidence (7.3 b); what can go wrong (7.3 d, f); detection (7.3 f); contain or recover (7.3 e); who accepts residual risk (7.3 d); unresolved dissent (7.3 h).
candidates.minimum_mechanism: No readiness record type and no readiness template. Readiness is the decision to proceed, written in a decision record with the assurance block. A project that wants a separate page uses the same block.
candidates.wording: No separate wording; clause 7.3 is the readiness rule. Guide sentence: 'A readiness or go/no-go statement is a decision to proceed; record it as a decision with the assurance block. The claim that the change is ready is a conclusion and needs its evidence; the choice to proceed needs its authority.'
candidates.could_amend: Clause 7.3 and templates/decision.md.
candidates.tradeoffs: Teams with an existing launch checklist tool must map it, not copy it. A decision record per significant deployment may feel heavy; the pull request description can be the record.
candidates.weakest_point: If the readiness record is just a decision record, a challenger can say M-13 was not adopted at all. That is accurate: the proposal rejects the object and keeps the questions.

admission.failure: Readiness cannot be reconstructed. Anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: A material claim has an identifiable basis.
admission.detection: Reading one page.
admission.cost: Nothing; no new object.

candidates.title: Exception object
candidates.problem: Exceptions are invisible, ownerless, and permanent by default.
candidates.failure_mode: A requirement is read as in force when it is not; an expired waiver keeps being relied on.
candidates.observed_case: Public: Rogers Commission, Chapter V finding 2 and Chapter VI (constraint waived flight after flight). Vaughan (not inspected) names the pattern. KADS: README adoption note has an Exceptions row; clause-examples.md shows 'Exception to clause 3.5.4(a)'. No adopter failure.
candidates.behavior: Exceptions are few, dated, owned, and easy to find.
candidates.rationale: KADS conformance already defines the exception with six fields. NPR 7120.5F adds the Non-Applicable disposition, which answers 'when is a permanent deviation legitimate': when the requirement cannot apply to the case; otherwise change the requirement.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.4. The exception is a decision record (type decision) with fixed field spellings; no new type, no new status (an expired exception is 'deprecated' or superseded by its renewal), no new relation. Of the eleven fields in the brief, id, status, and approved_by come from 4.2 and 4.6; evidence and mitigation are optional prose.
candidates.wording: 7.4 (a) An exception MUST identify the requirement departed from, its scope, the reason, the risk accepted, who accepted it, and an expiry date or review condition. (b) An exception stated to be permanent SHOULD say why the requirement is not changed instead. (c) An exception whose expiry date has passed without a recorded renewal MUST NOT be presented as in force. (d) Exceptions in force SHOULD be listed where the requirement is stated or be reachable from the corpus entry point. An exception to a KADS clause is the exception that conformance already requires; this clause adds no field to it.
candidates.could_amend: docs/conformance.md Review outcome carries the fields for KADS clauses. 7.4 adds expiry behaviour (c) and visibility (d).
candidates.tradeoffs: 'Expire unless renewed' is implemented as a rule about presentation, not about enforcement. Visibility is a SHOULD.
candidates.weakest_point: 7.4 (c) needs a date; an exception with only a review condition never trips it. That is the hole through which permanence returns.

admission.failure: A reader relies on a waived requirement or an expired waiver. Observed publicly.
admission.property: Current guidance can be found; a statement's scope is known.
admission.detection: Reading one page: fields present; expiry date compared with today and with any renewal note.
admission.cost: Nothing unless adopted; then known exceptions get an expiry or review condition.

candidates.title: Roles
candidates.problem: Records say 'approved' without saying who did what, so one person's signature reads as several independent checks.
candidates.failure_mode: Approval counts stand in for scrutiny.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: invented 'reviewed by the maintainer' statements corrected in 0.6.0. No adopter case.
candidates.behavior: Records name the people or roles behind acceptance, risk acceptance, and examination, and say when they are the same person.
candidates.rationale: Clause 4.6 already names the authority; 3.3.4 the author of record; 7.3 (d) and (g) the risk acceptor and the examiner. RFC 7282 is the precedent against counting.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: No role vocabulary. A paragraph in the decision guide: the five names in the brief are functions, one person may hold several, and the record says who held which. 'Challenger' is plain language for the examiner in 7.3 (g).
candidates.wording: No normative text. Guide paragraph: 'Author, reviewer, challenger, approver, and risk owner are functions, not posts. At lower levels one person may hold all of them. A record names who held each function that its level requires it to state, and says so when two are the same person or when one is an automated agent (clause 3.3.4). The number of approvers is not evidence.'
candidates.could_amend: docs/decision-guide.md.
candidates.tradeoffs: Without defined roles, projects will use different words. That is acceptable; KADS maps local terms elsewhere too.
candidates.weakest_point: Nothing normative results, so a challenger may ask why it is a candidate at all. It is kept as guidance because the profile's fields presuppose the functions.

admission.failure: Approval is mistaken for scrutiny. Observed in KADS history.
admission.property: Nothing is stated more firmly than its support.
admission.detection: Not a rule; no detection needed.
admission.cost: Nothing.

candidates.title: Incident learning loop
candidates.problem: Incident analysis is not connected to the decisions and assumptions it invalidates.
candidates.failure_mode: A decision record keeps an assumption that an incident disproved; the next reader trusts it.
candidates.observed_case: Public: GitLab 2017 lists improvement actions with owners. KADS: adopter lesson 3 produced clause 5.7 through a recorded disposition. No adopter failure case.
candidates.behavior: Incident authors link back to the decision or assumption that failed, and forward to the change.
candidates.rationale: The nomenclature already says that links to an assumption's question record 'are the review list when the question is answered against the assumption'. An incident is such an answer.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Clause 7.5 (a) carries the valid outcomes: of the brief's eight, six are 'change made' with different targets, plus 'risk accepted' and 'no change'; 'pending' is added for honesty. 7.5 (b) links to the affected decision. 7.5 (c) asks critical records to say when their outcome will be checked. The incident record is an investigation record.
candidates.wording: 7.5 (a) A record of an incident investigation MUST state, for each lesson it draws, one disposition: a change made, with a link to it; a change pending, with a link to where it is tracked; a risk accepted, naming who accepted it; or no change, with the reason. (b) Where an incident shows that an assumption or evidence relied on by a recorded decision did not hold, the incident record SHOULD link to that decision. (c) A record at the critical level SHOULD state when and how its outcome will be checked, and later what was observed.
candidates.could_amend: templates/investigation.md gains no section; a separate incident outline is offered because blameless framing and dispositions need prompts.
candidates.tradeoffs: 7.5 (b) and (c) are SHOULD because a reviewer cannot detect a missing link to a decision they do not know exists.
candidates.weakest_point: 7.5 (c), outcome follow-up, has no observed case and the weakest detection; it is the first item to drop if the profile must shrink.

admission.failure: Disproved assumptions stay in force. Anticipated in adoption.
admission.property: History is preserved; current guidance can be found.
admission.detection: (a) reading one page; (b) and (c) not reliably detectable, hence SHOULD.
admission.cost: Nothing unless adopted.

candidates.title: Typed relationships
candidates.problem: Assurance records need to point at evidence, assumptions, requirements, and each other in a way a reader and a text search can follow.
candidates.failure_mode: Links exist but their meaning is unclear, or eleven new relation names are added and nobody applies them consistently.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: J-018 rejected all relation additions in 0.6.0, with one recorded dissent (refines). No real document has yet shown a reading the existing eleven relations cannot express.
candidates.behavior: Authors use the existing vocabulary and two fixed field labels.
candidates.rationale: Admission question 7 demands a reader question and a real document. Nine of the eleven candidates are expressible today; two are fields of a record, not relations between records.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Add no relation. Mapping: decision supported-by evidence = supported-by or evidenced-by. Decision assumes assumption = depends-on a question record (already in the nomenclature). Decision supersedes decision = supersedes. Incident invalidates assumption = contradicts, and the question record is answered against the assumption. Incident changes requirement = the lesson is implemented-by the changed requirement; the requirement change is supported-by the incident. Incident produces evidence = inverse of evidenced-by. Readiness evaluates change = not needed, readiness is the decision; the decision is implemented-by the change. Dissent challenges decision = text in the record; a separate dissenting record contradicts the decision. Exception accepted-by authority = the authority field of clause 4.6, not a relation. Decision mitigates risk = text in 7.3 (d); if the risk is tracked as a question record, the decision answers it for a stated scope. Exception deviates-from requirement = the fixed field label 'Exception to:' with a link, a spelling KADS already uses in clause-examples.md.
candidates.wording: No normative text. One paragraph in registry/relationships.md, informative: the mapping above, and the fixed spelling 'Exception to:' so that a text search for it lists every exception.
candidates.could_amend: registry/relationships.md, advisory paragraph.
candidates.tradeoffs: 'Exception to:' is a relation in everything but name. Using 'answers' for mitigation stretches its meaning.
candidates.weakest_point: A challenger can fairly say deviates-from is the one case where the vocabulary cannot answer 'which exceptions exist against this requirement', and that a fixed label avoids the admission test instead of passing it. If so, the fallback is one relation, 'excepts', with required target, and nothing else.

admission.failure: Relation sprawl or unreadable links. Anticipated only.
admission.property: None broken today.
admission.detection: Search for the fixed label.
admission.cost: Nothing.

candidates.title: Architecture: Core versus addenda
candidates.problem: Five addenda would add five adoption decisions and overlapping fields; putting everything in Core would violate the brief.
candidates.failure_mode: Adopters cannot tell which parts apply; or Core users are forced into assurance practice.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: the Procedure profile of five clauses was dropped from 0.6.0 and all challengers found the draft too large; admission question 3 warns that 'a profile also adds a decision to every adoption'.
candidates.behavior: One opt-in decision, one place to read.
candidates.rationale: The five candidate addenda share one spine: a decision record whose content grows with level. Exceptions and incidents are the same record types KADS already has. One profile is therefore enough, and Core is untouched.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: One optional profile, specification section 7, 'Assurance profile', five clauses. One sentence added to clause 4.6. Everything else is guidance. The common core (section 3) receives no change.
candidates.wording: 7.1 Use this profile when a project wants a later reader to be able to reconstruct, for its consequential decisions, changes, exceptions, and incidents: what was believed, on what evidence, which risks were accepted and by whom, and what happened afterwards. The profile states what a record makes discoverable. It does not require that a review be held, that a role be staffed, or that a change be approved (clause 3.6.3), and it requires nothing for a decision or change at the routine level. It can be used with or without tracked records.
candidates.could_amend: Section 4 could host 7.3 to 7.5 as clauses 4.7 to 4.9, avoiding a new profile. Rejected because it would bind every tracked-record adopter to assurance content.
candidates.tradeoffs: A third profile is a third adoption decision. Five clauses equal the size of the Procedure profile that was dropped.
candidates.weakest_point: The last round removed a profile of exactly this size for thin evidence, and this one rests on public incidents, not adopter cases. The honest fallback is: 4.6 sentence plus guidance only, with the profile text kept as a recorded deferred proposal.

admission.failure: Assurance content either leaks into Core or fragments. Observed in KADS history as the reason the previous draft was cut.
admission.property: Not a corpus property; a design constraint.
admission.detection: Reading the adoption note for the profile declaration.
admission.cost: Nothing for existing corpora except the 4.6 sentence if they use tracked decisions.

candidates.title: Templates
candidates.problem: Without prompts, authors forget fields; with four new templates, the same decision gets written four times.
candidates.failure_mode: Document proliferation; abandoned templates.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: the templates directory already has eleven outlines. Anticipated only.
candidates.behavior: Authors add a block to a record they already write.
candidates.rationale: The brief prefers a section or metadata block over a separate document.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: One assurance block inserted into the existing decision and ADR outlines (this is the Decision and the Readiness template), one exception outline, one incident outline. Two new files, one amended.
candidates.wording: No normative text. Full template text is in the integrated design, part (e).
candidates.could_amend: templates/decision.md and templates/adr.md gain the block; templates/investigation.md could carry the incident outline but its prompts differ enough to justify a file.
candidates.tradeoffs: Two more files in a directory of eleven.
candidates.weakest_point: The incident outline could be a section of the investigation outline; a minimalist challenger will say so and is probably right.

admission.failure: Missing fields or duplicated documents. Anticipated only.
admission.property: None; templates are informative.
admission.detection: Not applicable.
admission.cost: Nothing.

candidates.title: Lifecycle states for KADS's own principles
candidates.problem: A rule that merely sounds reasonable becomes normative and is then hard to remove.
candidates.failure_mode: KADS accumulates clauses with no operational evidence and no review date.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: three 0.6.0 rules were adopted with wording the six challengers never saw, one with no observed failure (3.3.4 addition), as the standards evaluation records. The limits section says most changes rest on argument.
candidates.behavior: Every clause admitted without an observed case carries that fact and a reopening condition where a reader of the changelog sees it.
candidates.rationale: RFC 2026 separates designation from operational experience and has an Experimental category. KADS already has: decision statuses proposed, accepted, rejected, superseded; a 'Reopen when' column; admission question 1 ('observed or anticipated only').
candidates.minimum_mechanism: No new statuses. One sentence in CONTRIBUTING and one column in the changelog entry: basis observed or anticipated. 'Challenged' and 'revised' are events, not states; 'experimental' is expressed as 'anticipated only, review at the next minor release after the first adopter report'.
candidates.wording: CONTRIBUTING, after the admission test: 'A rule admitted on an anticipated failure only is listed as such in the changelog with the condition that will trigger its review. Until an observed case is recorded it is a candidate for removal at each release review.'
candidates.could_amend: CONTRIBUTING.md, Admission test section; the changelog format.
candidates.tradeoffs: No status means no single word to search for. The whole section 7 would itself be 'anticipated only' in adoption.
candidates.weakest_point: Six states were asked for and none is delivered; a challenger can say the candidate is rejected in substance. It is, on admission question 7: no reader question arose in a real document that 'proposed, accepted, superseded' plus a reopen condition cannot answer.

admission.failure: Unevidenced rules become permanent. Observed in KADS's own evaluation limits.
admission.property: Nothing is stated more firmly than its support (applied to KADS itself).
admission.detection: Reading the changelog entry.
admission.cost: Nothing for adopters.

candidates.title: Dogfooding evidence
candidates.problem: KADS has one adopter and no routine for learning whether its rules help.
candidates.failure_mode: Rules stay because nobody asked whether they still earn their place.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: docs/reviews/2026-10-02-adoption-feedback.md is the only adoption evidence; decisions/standards/README.md, Limits, says so.
candidates.behavior: At each release the maintainer asks of each clause with a fired reopening condition: would we add this today? Deletion is recorded as a valid outcome.
candidates.rationale: The SRE launch checklist needs 'continuous attention' and prunes obsolete items. CONTRIBUTING already says requirements are reviewed 'when an adoption exposes ambiguity'.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Two sentences in CONTRIBUTING under Review route, and the ten signals of the brief listed in the adoption guide as optional things an adopter may report. No metrics requirement, no tooling.
candidates.wording: CONTRIBUTING, Review route: 'Before each minor release, review every clause whose reopening condition has occurred and every clause still marked anticipated only, asking whether it would be added today. Retiring a clause is a valid outcome and is recorded like any other decision.'
candidates.could_amend: CONTRIBUTING.md, Review route.
candidates.tradeoffs: Without measurement the review is opinion. With one adopter there is little signal.
candidates.weakest_point: Signals such as 'time to locate decisions' cannot be collected without instrumentation KADS refuses to require; the list may be decoration.

admission.failure: The standard grows monotonically. Anticipated; the previous draft's size is the nearest observed case.
admission.property: Not a corpus property.
admission.detection: Reading the release's review record.
admission.cost: Nothing for adopters.

candidates.title: Complexity accounting per version
candidates.problem: Growth of the standard is invisible release to release.
candidates.failure_mode: Each release adds a little; nobody sees the total.
candidates.observed_case: KADS history: the 0.6.0 changelog already carries a table of clauses and keyword counts for 0.5.0 and 0.6.0 (43 to 48 clauses, 64 to 68 MUST), and CONTRIBUTING release step 2 already asks for 'the clause and keyword counts'.
candidates.behavior: The maintainer sees and publishes the net change in every release.
candidates.rationale: The practice exists and was the instrument by which the previous draft was judged too large.
candidates.minimum_mechanism: Extend the existing table: add defined terms, record types, statuses, relations, templates, and a removed column. One edited sentence in CONTRIBUTING release step 2.
candidates.wording: CONTRIBUTING release step 2, replace 'the clause and keyword counts' with: 'the counts of clauses, keywords, defined terms, record types, statuses, relations, and templates, each as added and removed'.
candidates.could_amend: CONTRIBUTING.md release steps; CHANGELOG.md table.
candidates.tradeoffs: Counts are a proxy; a single long clause can hide much. Required-field counts are judgment calls.
candidates.weakest_point: It is already done; the increment is small enough that a challenger may call it a patch, not a candidate.

admission.failure: Unnoticed growth. Observed: the previous draft.
admission.property: Not a corpus property.
admission.detection: Reading the changelog table.
admission.cost: Nothing for adopters.
